explanation: Fires strongest on ' respectively' after a list of paired numbers or percentages in scientific text (e.g. '1.8 and 0.2 percent respectively'). Also fires on a scattered mix of other tokens that finish a fixed phrase ('so far so', 'friend of', 'in question', 'don't delay', 'amicus', 'implements Comparable'). Elsewhere it fires weakly.

Fires inside technical or scientific compound terms, mostly in chemistry and biomedical abstracts. Typical spots are the commas between locants in chemical names ('1,2-diols'), isotope labels ('[99mTc]', '[3H]') and adverb suffixes such as 'urally', 'arily' and 'ically' in 'structurally' or 'evolutionarily'. It also fires on 'and' in coordinated adjectives ('temporary, and voluntary'). It is weak in ordinary prose.

Fires strongly on action verbs that advance a narrative ('came back', 'steps back', 'slowed') and on pronouns or 'and' at those points. It also fires on the last seconds digit of timestamps in logs and subtitles ('18:06:59', '00:00:56') and on the space before a voltage number ('TTL 3.3 V'). These look like unrelated jobs.

No clear meaning. It fires on many different tokens: thousands-separator commas ('350,000'), commas in diff hunk headers ('+3771,17'), the second part of a split word ('Lactoc-occus', 'quick-cou-pling'), and on 'the', 'Less' and 'Hyper'. The examples share no visible pattern.

Fires mostly on function words that come right after a noun subject or object, especially 'is', 'as', 'in' and 'of' ('Set data is', 'difficulty is', 'Prynt is', 'main goal of'). It also fires on assorted other tokens. The pattern is diffuse.

Fires on a word-piece in the first or middle part of a rare proper noun or unusual word that the tokenizer splits up ('f-ore-castle', 'Syl-ve-on', 're-k-ognition', 'Ale-k-sey', 'I-liamna', 'Mal-ala', '-le-ader'). Activation is highest at the start of a name, and the meaning of the word does not matter.

Fires on non-Latin-script tokens (Japanese, Chinese, Devanagari, Cyrillic, Arabic), especially when such script appears inside or right after English or code context (Chinese comments in code, the native-script name in brackets after an English name). It fires weakly to moderately on English nouns for people or groups ('Republicans', 'spokesman', 'Texans').

Fires on the second piece of a word or name that the tokenizer splits, where the rest of the word is mostly predictable ('Black-pool', 'Midloth-ian', 'M-ale', 'Fol-ks', 'En-field', 'O'Le-ary', 'trans-duction'). It also fires on some tokens that continue code syntax ('.set(', 'self.'). The pattern is broad.

Fires on nationality adjectives and occupation context in short biographies, mainly the nationality word in 'was a German botanist' or 'born 1943, Argentine footballer'. It also fires on 'became', 'a former' and 'worked as a' in career descriptions. It fires on the inner pieces of long Romance-language words ('univers-it-ário', 'com-unit-ario') as well.

Fires on word-pieces inside words from languages other than English (Norwegian, Romanian, Finnish, Albanian, German, Hindi, Samoan names) and inside misspelled or oddly split English words ('us-i-ng', 'More-ver', 'parl-iment', 'IM-HO', 'BT-W'). It fires on pieces that continue a word, not on whole common English words.

Fires on the last piece that completes a technical word, name or identifier, usually a suffix ('benzophen-one', 'naltrex-one', 'Khron-os', 'Baron-et', 'CIRCU-IT', 'MISSISSIP-PI', 'E-select-in', '__esModule'). It is weaker on ordinary words.

Fires in sports and statistics text on tokens for stats or roles ('577 passing yards', 'first Grade appearance', '16-down', '42 points', 'played for'). It also fires on '+/-' in mean ± SD statistics and on '\ldots' or commas in lists of mathematical vectors. These are several loosely related numeric and list contexts.

Fires strongest on 'No' in the patent citation 'U.S. Pat. No.'. It also fires on tokens at the end of citations and legal or identifier strings, such as 'GPL-2.0', 'pone.0153' and 'TEXAS' in court headers, and on the 'H' or 'h' after an elided d' in French ('d'Histoire'). Other text gives little activation.

Fires on words about results, outcomes or benefits in medical and marketing text ('excellent long-term results', 'significant savings', 'short-term', 'good result', 'poorer prognosis', 'improve'). It peaks on evaluative or result words and qualifiers just before 'outcome', 'results' or 'savings'.

Fires on a function word that opens a common idiom or clause frame and commits to what follows: 'from' in 'vary, from' or '- from', 'once in a lifetime', 'If you can' or 'If you want', 'a copy of which', 'at least', 'and later'. There is no tight semantic theme, so this is a diffuse role tied to structure.

Fires on the second half of a contrast or comparison, on the word that states the opposite or different outcome: 'hypoactivation ... and hyperactivation', 'exclude ... but must include', 'whereas no apoptosis', 'not guilty', 'did not inhibit', 'the loss for Penn'. Activation is highest right after 'whereas', 'while', 'but' or 'not'.

No clear meaning. It fires on a mix of function words and nouns mid-sentence ('if', 'the', 'in', 'to', 'not', 'remainder', 'value', 'references') in explanatory or question-and-answer text. There is no consistent token or context.

Fires on the preposition 'to' when it marks a recipient, goal or attachment after a verb or noun ('chained himself to', 'delivered to', 'make sense to me', 'supplied to', 'a kick to', 'assigned to'). It does not fire on the infinitive 'to'.

Fires inside synthetic math problems (DeepMind-style 'Let p be h(0)'), mainly on 'be' in 'Let x be ...', on '/(-' division signs, on operators and minus signs after 'Suppose', and on the parenthesis in function calls like 'z(3)'. Outside such problems it is near zero.

Fires on the second token of a fixed technical multi-word term or name, mostly statistics or methods ('likelihood ratio', 'proportional hazards', 'principal component', 'slow wave', 'tissue microarray', 'MR fingerprinting'). It also fires on second tokens in code ('STAThread', 'argc', '<' after a class name in Objective-C).

Fires on the token 'but' (as a word or the first piece of 'butler', 'butyl', 'Butland', 'butts'), with peaks on the 'but WITHOUT ANY WARRANTY' license phrase. It also fires on 'But' or 'And' at the start of a line after a code block in Q&A posts. Plain 'and' as a coordinator gets weak to moderate activation.
